newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open firm following overseas trend.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open firm following overseas trend.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Monday, following overseas trends.
The only economic report due out one on July consumer installment credit. Economists estimate that credit expanded by $7.2 billion in July, after growing $8.3 billion in June.
"The Producer Price Index on Thursday and the Consumer Price Index and retail sales data on Friday will be the focus this week," said MCM Moneywatch economist James Blumenthal.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark T-bond was quoted up 4/32 at 95-22/32, yielding 7.10 percent in early trade.

Analysts at MMS International said Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer's remarks to the National Association of Business Economists in Boston on Sunday were on the supportive side for the Treasury market.

Meyer said there were some signs that the economy was slowing in the second half of the year and he said that one single report, even as strong as the U.S. August employment report, does not determine the outcome of a policy-setting meeting. The government said Friday that U.S. non-farm payrolls expanded by 250,000 jobs in August and that average hourly earnings rose six cents an hour.
The Labor Department also said the jobless rate fell to 5.1 percent (5.4 percent in July), the lowest since March 1989 when the jobless rate was 5.0 percent.

Economists had forecast payrolls would post a rise of 244,000 in August, while the unemployment rate was seen at 5.3 percent and on Friday, analysts said the report dramatically increased the chances for a monetary policy tightening by the Federal Reserve in September.
On Sunday, Meyer said the Fed keeps hearing anecdotal evidence about "tight labor markets and scattered wage increases" but said inflation remains at a steady, low rate.

But Meyer said the Fed was focusing on the large payroll gain in August coupled with the low 5.1 percent unemployment rate that is "outside of the range of the last two years," in combination with a lengthening workweek and higher earnings.
Blumenthal said that "although it's by no means certain, the market concensus is leaning towards the idea that the Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points" at its September policy meeting.
"That doesn't mean the view might not change," he said. "That's one reason the inflation data at the end of the week are very important - coming after the Friday employment data."

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month Treasury bill rates were unchanged at 5.19 percent. Six-month rates were down one basis point to 5.34 percent. The one-year bill rate was unchanged at 5.58 percent.

The two-year note was unchanged at 99-20/32, yielding 6.35 percent. The five-year note was unchanged at 99-05/32, yielding 6.70 percent, and the 10-year note was unchanged at 100-16/32, yielding 6.93 percent.
